messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 39

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no bullet points.

Ravi Patel, a 58-year-old South Asian American bomb disposal technician, had always seen himself as someone who could stay calm when others could not. For more than three decades he had built a career around careful preparation, steady hands, and the ability to face danger without showing it. That sense of competence was shattered four years ago when his 19-year-old son, Arjun, developed a rapidly worsening infection that progressed into septic shock within hours. Ravi remembers the emergency room in fragments: the harsh fluorescent lights, the sound of monitors beeping in uneven rhythms, the surgeon’s tight expression, his wife’s silent crying at the end of the bed. The most searing moment came when Arjun’s breathing became shallow and he was rushed for intubation. Ravi stood outside the room, unable to do anything, and the helplessness felt intolerable. In the days that followed, as his son remained in the ICU, Ravi found himself replaying the scene repeatedly, convinced that if he had noticed the fever sooner, pushed harder for earlier care, or trusted his instincts rather than waiting for the pediatrician’s reassurance, Arjun might not have come so close to dying.

Although Arjun survived, the experience left Ravi changed in ways that became more apparent after he returned to work. At first he told himself he simply needed to “get back to normal,” but he began having intrusive images of his son’s limp body on the hospital bed, often when he was driving to the base or sitting in his truck before a call. He would suddenly feel as though he were back in the ICU, chest tight and palms damp, with a rush of dread that something terrible was about to happen again. On the job, when his team entered a scene with a child present or even a report involving a school bus, Ravi’s mind would jump immediately to the hospital and to the possibility of losing his own son. He became more irritable and tense, startling at unexpected noises in the garage, and he noticed that his sleep had become lighter and more broken. He woke often at 3 or 4 a.m. with his heart pounding, scanning the house to make sure Arjun was safe, even though Arjun was now an adult living nearby.

Ravi’s avoidance developed quietly and then widened. He stopped visiting the ICU floor whenever he had to drive his wife to appointments at the medical center, and he found excuses not to attend neighborhood gatherings where people asked after Arjun. He avoided conversations with parents whose children were sick, because hearing about fevers, surgeries, or hospitalizations made him feel suddenly nauseated and guilty. At work, he delegated more of the emotionally charged tasks involving children to younger colleagues when he could, telling himself that he needed to be “efficient,” though privately he feared that seeing another family in that kind of crisis would undo him. He also avoided his own emotions, particularly any moment that might lead him to think about how frightened Arjun must have been. When his wife tried to talk about those days, Ravi changed the subject or became focused on practical details, because allowing himself to feel the grief and fear seemed dangerous; he worried that if he fully opened the memory, he would be overwhelmed and never regain control.

Over time, Ravi’s beliefs about safety and responsibility became harsher. He began to see himself as someone who had failed in the one role that mattered most, a father who should have protected his child and did not. Although Arjun had recovered physically, Ravi could not shake the conviction that the world was fragile and that disaster could strike without warning, especially in the lives of the people he loved. He became hypervigilant at home, checking Arjun’s texts repeatedly and listening for any change in his voice on the phone. He was easily jumpy and had trouble concentrating during long drives to job sites, where he would catch himself imagining ambulances, hospital corridors, and his son’s face when he had been too sick to speak. His colleagues noticed that he was more withdrawn, less willing to linger after calls, and more likely to snap when interrupted. He felt ashamed of needing so much reassurance and interpreted his own reactions as weakness, which only deepened his sense of isolation.

Ravi sought help after Arjun was hospitalized overnight for a severe asthma exacerbation, a relatively minor event medically but one that threw Ravi back into the same terror with full force. He spent the night pacing the hallway outside Arjun’s room, unable to sleep, convinced that the next phone call could be the one that brought catastrophic news. By the next morning he knew he could not keep functioning this way. He came to treatment hoping to stop the vivid reliving, to sleep through the night, and to trust that his son’s safety was not entirely in his hands. More than anything, Ravi is afraid that if anything happens again he will freeze, fail, or be consumed by guilt, and he is most hoping to find a way to feel like a steady father again without living as though disaster is always about to happen.
